answer_text:
Let

\[
a_n(x)=\frac{(\sin x)^n}{x^n}=\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^n,\qquad x>0.
\]

### 1. Pointwise limit

For every \(x>0\),

\[
\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le 1,
\]

and in fact the inequality is strict for all \(x>0\), since \(|\sin x|<x\) near \(0\) and \(|\sin x|\le 1<x\) for sufficiently large \(x\). Hence

\[
\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|<1 \qquad \text{for all } x>0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^n=0
\]

for every fixed \(x\in(0,\infty)\). Thus the pointwise limit is

\[
f(x)=0,\qquad x\in(0,\infty).
\]

### 2. Application of the Dominated Convergence Theorem

For \(n\ge 2\),

\[
|a_n(x)|
=
\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|^n
\le
\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|^2
=
\frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}.
\]

Define

\[
g(x)=\frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}.
\]

We check that \(g\) is integrable on \((0,\infty)\). For \(0<x\le 1\),

\[
0\le g(x)\le 1,
\]

so

\[
\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx\le 1.
\]

For \(x\ge 1\),

\[
0\le g(x)\le \frac{1}{x^2},
\]

so

\[
\int_1^\infty g(x)\,dx\le \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1.
\]

Hence \(g\in L^1(0,\infty)\).

Since \(a_n(x)\to 0\) pointwise and \(|a_n(x)|\le g(x)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), the Dominated Convergence Theorem gives

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^\infty a_n(x)\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n(x)\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty 0\,dx
=
0.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
